explanations.answer: They stumbled because of their sin
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The call says, "…for you have stumbled by your iniquity." Stumbled, like a toe catching the edge of the rug. I've tripped over my own mustache more times than I can count, so I know that feeling. And the way back is named in the very same breath: "Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God…"

explanations.answer: They were scattered by their enemies
explanations.explanation: The call never brings up enemies at all. It says Israel "stumbled by" their "iniquity." That's the reason it gives for coming back. Hold onto that word stumbled, because it matters in this passage.

explanations.answer: They were misled by their kings
explanations.explanation: No kings in this verse, friend. The call points to Israel's own iniquity: "…you have stumbled by your iniquity." I once blamed the oven for a flat batch, and the oven just sat there looking innocent. Here the verse skips the blame game and goes straight to the invitation to return.

Yes, confessions. The verse says, "Bring your confessions and return to the LORD." Confessions are the very thing it names. I think that's a comfort for anybody who ever walked into a room with empty pockets.

No silver in this verse, friend. What Israel is told to bring is their confessions: "Bring your confessions and return to the LORD." Nobody has to make a shopping trip first. Honest words are what the verse asks for.
No herd required here. The verse says, "Bring your confessions and return to the LORD." Confessions fit in anybody's hands, and they don't need a trailer. The call asks for words, plain and honest.

All of it! The words say, "Take away all our iniquity…" Not a piece of it, not the easy part. I love that the words they're given hand the whole pile over. When you're sweeping up a mess, the broom works best when you stop hiding crumbs under the rug.
Close, but the words say more than that. They ask, "Take away all our iniquity…" It's like cleaning the whole kitchen and leaving one corner for later. This request leaves no corner behind.
The words don't sort the iniquity into worst and not so bad. They say, "Take away all our iniquity…" Every bit of it goes on the table. I think that's the honest way to ask.
That's it. In the words Israel is given, they say, "Assyria will not save us, nor will we ride on horses." Assyria is the name those words pick. I think that's a big thing to say out loud.
Egypt isn't named in these words, friend. The verse says, "Assyria will not save us…" Keep that name in your pocket.
Babylon isn't named here. The words Israel is given say, "Assyria will not save us, nor will we ride on horses." The verse picks Assyria, and that's the one that counts.
True. The words say, "We will never again say, ‘Our gods!’ to the work of our own hands." Israel is given those words to say. I think that takes courage.

The words actually say the opposite of that. Israel is told to say, "We will never again say, ‘Our gods!’ to the work of our own hands." So it's a promise to leave that behind. The statement on the card was true, friend.

The fatherless, yes. The words end with, "For in You the fatherless find compassion." That's the line they close on. I know a little about being left in the dark and then found, so this line lands with me.
The verse doesn't say the mighty. It says, "For in You the fatherless find compassion." Compassion goes toward the ones who have no father to look after them. The reason isn't power, friend.
Wealthy doesn't show up in this verse. The words say, "For in You the fatherless find compassion." The ones named are the fatherless. Nobody here is asked for a bank statement.
Heal it! The LORD says, "I will heal their apostasy…" Apostasy is turning away from Him. His answer is healing. Friend, I'd have taken a long pause here too, because that's some good news.

Not in this verse. The LORD says, "I will heal their apostasy; I will freely love them…" Apostasy is turning away from Him. The next words say, "…for My anger has turned away from them." So the answer is healing.
Nothing about exposing here, friend. The LORD says, "I will heal their apostasy…" Apostasy is turning away from Him. He goes on to say, "I will freely love them…"
Not quite, friend. The LORD says, "I will freely love them…" Freely means no price tag. Love that has to be earned isn't what this verse says.

False, and I'm so glad. The LORD says, "I will freely love them, for My anger has turned away from them." Freely, friend, with no earning. I like a cookie cooling on the rack, and no one has to pay admission to love it.
Anger. The LORD says, "I will freely love them, for My anger has turned away from them." That's the reason He gives. I'm over a burnt batch in about ten minutes, so I admire this.
Close, but it's not the word here. The verse says, "…for My anger has turned away from them." So the thing that has turned away is His anger. The love is free, and that's the reason He gives.
Patience isn't what the verse says has turned away. It says, "I will freely love them, for My anger has turned away from them." So it's His anger that turned. I'm glad the verse puts it that plainly.

Dew! The LORD says, "I will be like the dew to Israel…" I think dew is a gentle picture, though that's my own thought. The verse just says dew and then goes straight to blossoming. A picture like that makes me want to open the bakery window.
The verse doesn't pick wind. The LORD says, "I will be like the dew to Israel…" Dew is what He names. Then comes, "he will blossom like the lily…"
Not fire here, friend. The LORD says, "I will be like the dew to Israel; he will blossom like the lily…" Dew is the picture. And right after it comes blossoming.

Not in this verse, friend. The LORD says Israel "…will blossom like the lily and take root like the cedars of Lebanon." That's blossoming, not withering. This picture goes up and down at the same time.
False. The LORD says Israel "…will blossom like the lily and take root like the cedars of Lebanon." Blossoming on top and roots underneath. Nobody in this picture is wilting in the sun.
Grain! The verse says, "They will return and dwell in his shade; they will grow grain and blossom like the vine." It's a picture of growth. Friend, that's a lot of good in one verse.
No thorns in this picture. The verse says, "They will return and dwell in his shade; they will grow grain and blossom like the vine." What grows is grain. It's a picture of growth, not of prickles.
Figs are a fine fruit, but the verse names something else. It says, "they will grow grain and blossom like the vine." So the answer is grain. The vine shows up in the next breath.
True. The LORD says, "O Ephraim, what have I to do anymore with idols? It is I who answer and watch over him." He speaks to Ephraim here. He says He is the One who answers and watches over him.
It's the other way around. The LORD says, "O Ephraim, what have I to do anymore with idols? It is I who answer and watch over him." So the statement on the card was true.
From Him. The LORD says, "I am like a flourishing cypress; your fruit comes from Me." Ephraim's fruit has a source, and the LORD names Himself as it. I'd frame that on my bakery wall.
Cedars of Lebanon show up earlier, as a picture of Israel taking root. Here the LORD says, "I am like a flourishing cypress; your fruit comes from Me." So the source He names is Himself, not a tree.

That's not what the verse says, friend. The LORD says, "I am like a flourishing cypress; your fruit comes from Me." He names Himself as the source. I'll still proudly stamp a good cookie, but I know where the good things come from.

Right. The verse says, "For the ways of the LORD are right, and the righteous walk in them but the rebellious stumble in them." That's the last thing this whole passage leaves you with. The righteous walk and the rebellious stumble, and we heard that word in the very first verse.
Hidden isn't the word. The verse says, "For the ways of the LORD are right…" Right is the word it uses. And the verse says the righteous walk in them.

Narrow isn't what this verse says. It says, "For the ways of the LORD are right, and the righteous walk in them but the rebellious stumble in them." The word it uses is right. The righteous walk in them, and the rebellious stumble.
